herkunft.metaTitel: Coffee Cup Reading History: Where It Comes From | Tarot Cup
herkunft.metaBeschreibung: From Yemen to Istanbul and on to London and Vienna: the story of Turkish coffee and what is known about the age of coffee cup reading.
herkunft.titel: Where coffee cup reading comes from
kurzantwort: Coffee cup reading is part of the coffee culture that developed in the Ottoman Empire from the 16th century on: it takes finely ground, unfiltered Turkish coffee to leave grounds in the cup in which you can see shapes. How long people have been reading these grounds, on the other hand, is hardly documented; there is no reliable starting date. In the 17th century, coffee spread through Europe as a trade good and with the first coffeehouses, reaching London and Vienna, among other cities.

abschnitte.titel: How did coffee reach the Ottoman Empire?
absaetze: The story does not begin in Istanbul but on the Horn of Africa. The coffee plant comes from Ethiopia, where it was first used as food. As a drink, coffee spread in Yemen toward the end of the 15th century, first among Sufis: they valued it because it kept them refreshed and awake during prayer and the communal remembrance of God.

At the beginning of the 16th century, coffee reached Mecca and Cairo. From the ports on the Red Sea it traveled on through Egypt to Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire. Exactly when coffee reached Istanbul is disputed. The scholar Kâtib Çelebi reports that coffee arrived in the city by ship in 1543 and met resistance because of legal opinions against it; but it was probably drunk there earlier. Other Ottoman authors place the first coffeehouses about ten years later, between 1553 and 1555.

abschnitte.titel: When did the first coffeehouses open in Istanbul?
absaetze: A charming founding story has been handed down: the historian Peçuylu İbrâhim relates that two men, Hakem from Aleppo and Şems from Damascus, opened the first coffeehouses in the Istanbul district of Tahtakale around 1554 or 1555. Another author gives the year 1553. The beginning is usually placed in the first half of the 1550s.

The coffeehouse, called kahvehane in Turkish, quickly became more than a place to drink. People met to talk, exchanged news, listened to storytellers, or watched the Karagöz shadow play. Not everyone liked this. Some scholars objected to gossip, loose talk, and gambling, and the authorities above all feared talk about the state and the government. Coffeehouses were therefore banned again and again, but the bans rarely lasted long. Sultan Murad IV was especially strict: in 1633 he had the coffeehouses in Istanbul closed.
Still, coffee won out in the long run. The traveler Evliya Çelebi later counted around 500 coffee merchants and 300 coffee shops in the city.

What matters for reading is how Turkish coffee is made. Freshly roasted beans are ground very fine and heated slowly with cold water, and with sugar if you like, in a small pot until foam forms. The coffee is drunk unfiltered from small cups and served with a glass of water. Because nothing is filtered out, the grounds, telve in Turkish, stay behind in the cup at the end.

In 2013, UNESCO inscribed Turkish coffee culture and tradition on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The entry describes coffee as a sign of hospitality and friendship, an occasion for intimate conversation, and an established part of occasions such as engagements and holidays. It also mentions reading the grounds in the empty cup as part of this culture.

abschnitte.titel: How old is coffee cup reading itself?
absaetze: This is where things get uncertain. For the coffeehouses, there are chronicles with names and dates; for reading the cup, there are hardly any. Even detailed reference works on the Ottoman history of coffee and coffeehouses do not mention the custom. Two Italian authors who have written about coffee in 17th- and 18th-century Europe suspect that, when it comes to the origins of reading coffee grounds, what has been handed down and what is simply a pretty story can hardly be separated.

It is often said that the custom began in the sultan’s palace, for instance among the women of the harem. This is a widespread story, but the sources of this page offer no evidence for it. Only one simple point is certain: only what remains in the cup can be read. Coffee grounds can only be read where coffee is drunk unfiltered, so reading coffee grounds specifically cannot be older than this coffee culture. Even earlier, people looked into mirrors, water, or cups to read something from them, in Byzantium for example; whether coffee cup reading builds on this is not documented.
The guide [Coffee cup reading](/en/coffee-cup-reading/#was-ist-kaffeesatzlesen) describes what happens during a reading and how the ritual goes.

From the Ottoman Empire, coffee reached Europe through Mediterranean trade, arriving first in port cities such as Venice and Marseille. About a century after the first coffeehouses in Istanbul, major European cities had coffeehouses, too. The word itself traces the route: coffee goes back via the Turkish kahve to the Arabic qahwa.

In London, Pasqua Rosée opened a coffeehouse in 1652 in an alley beside the church of St Michael in Cornhill. He is described as Greek; he was the servant of an English merchant in the Levant trade who was fond of coffee himself. In the 18th century, there were already several hundred coffeehouses in London.

Vienna likes to tell a different story: after the siege by the Ottoman army in 1683, the scout Georg Franz Kolschitzky is said to have been granted the right to open the city’s first coffeehouse as a reward. This story is considered a legend; it was not written down until about a hundred years later. What is documented, however, is that on January 17, 1685, Johannes Diodato, an Armenian merchant from Istanbul, received the right to prepare coffee, tea, and sherbet for twenty years. With this, he opened the city’s first coffeehouse.

abschnitte.titel: What remains of the old custom?
absaetze: Today, the cup is often read within a close circle, for example among female friends. According to UNESCO, families pass on the knowledge surrounding coffee through watching and joining in.

A linguistic study from 2025 analyzed recordings of 22 such sessions among Turkish-speaking women who are friends. It shows that much of the talk in these sessions is about worries, and that reading together strengthens the bond between them.

Perhaps this is the real heart of the custom. The cup gives people a reason to sit together and talk about wishes and plans. A reading shows a possibility, not a fixed fate. The small customs that go with it, from the ring on the cup to the thumbprint, are described under [Customs of coffee cup reading](/en/coffee-cup-reading/#braeuche-beim-kaffeesatzlesen).

fragen.frage: Was coffee cup reading already practiced in the Ottoman Empire?
antwort: The custom is closely linked with Ottoman coffee culture, but there is no reliable starting date. The reference works on the history of coffee and coffeehouses that this page draws on do not mention it.

fragen.frage: How long have there been coffeehouses in Istanbul?
antwort: Ottoman historians give the years 1553 to 1555 for the first coffeehouses. According to tradition, two men from Aleppo and Damascus opened them in the Tahtakale district.

fragen.frage: Did Kolschitzky open the first coffeehouse in Vienna?
antwort: That story is often told, but it is considered a legend. What is documented is that in January 1685 the Armenian merchant Johannes Diodato became the first to receive the right to prepare coffee in Vienna, and so opened the city’s first coffeehouse.

fragen.frage: Why is Turkish coffee part of UNESCO’s cultural heritage?
antwort: In 2013, UNESCO inscribed not a drink but a whole culture: the preparation, the shared drinking, the hospitality, and the conversations around the cup.

fragen.frage: Why doesn’t coffee cup reading work with filter coffee?
antwort: When coffee is filtered, the grounds stay in the filter and not in the cup. A cup can only be read with finely ground coffee that is drunk unfiltered, as with Turkish coffee.

text: If you would like to look into your own cup after your coffee, Tarot Cup can guide you: you choose the symbols you recognize and place them where they appear in your cup.
